rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ʿafw can denote excess; the cited description of sheep as fat-rich supports the sense of surplus.
rows.anchor: ولكنا يعض السيف منا بأسوق عافيات الشحم كوم أي زائدات الشحم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ʿafw can also mean what is left or relinquished; the Prophet’s waived horse alms illustrate property one can dispense with.
rows.anchor: أي تركتها فيكون العفو المتروك غنى عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mukhalata is joining so closely that separation is difficult, like vinegar in water; partners are called khalitan because their property is mixed, and a khalit shares one common affair.
rows.anchor: والمخالطة مجامعة يتعذر معها التمييز كمخالطة الخل للماء وما أشبهه والخليطان الشريكان لاختلاط أموالهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iʿnat is imposing an unbearable hardship; the root denotes severity and distress.
rows.anchor: والإعنات الحمل على مشقة لا تطاق ثقلا وعنت العظم عنتا أصابه وهن أو كسر بعد جبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The governing word for “in this world and the hereafter” is يبين; it may instead depend on تتفكرون.
rows.anchor: العامل في الطرف من قوله في الدنيا والآخرة قوله يبين أي مبين لكم الآيات في أمر الدنيا والآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fa-ikhwanukum is preferably nominative as the predicate of an omitted “they are”; an accusative reading can mean “your brothers mix with you.”
rows.anchor: وقوله فإخوانكم رفع على أنه خبر مبتدأ محذوف وتقديره فهم إخوانكم

rows.speaker: جماعة من الصحابة
rows.claim: A group of Companions asked the Prophet about wine and gambling because they destroy reason and strip away wealth; this verse was revealed in response.
rows.anchor: نزلت في جماعة من الصحابة أتوا رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم فقالوا أفتنا في الخمر والميسر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent sense in Imami reports, also adopted by al-Shafiʿi, is any intoxicating drink that covers the mind; even a little is forbidden if much intoxicates.
rows.anchor: وهي كل شراب مسكر مخالط للعقل مغط عليه

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abu Hanifa restricts khamr to grape juice once it ferments and becomes strong.
rows.anchor: وقيل الخمر عصير العنب إذا اشتد وغلى وهو مذهب أبي حنيفة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وابن مسعود ومجاهد وقتادة والحسن
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, Ibn Masʿud, Mujahid, Qatada, and al-Hasan say maysir means all gambling; Imami reports count children’s nut games as gambling too.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس وابن مسعود ومجاهد وقتادة والحسن وهو المروي عن أئمتنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kabir here means a great and abundant burden of sin.
rows.anchor: أي وزر عظيم وكثير من الكثرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wine’s benefits were its sale proceeds and the pleasure, exhilaration, and strength people thought drinking brought.
rows.anchor: منفعة الخمر ما كانوا يأخذونه في أثمانها وما يحصل من اللذة والطرب والقوة بشربها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gambling’s benefit was winning another person’s money without labor or hardship, with the winner able to support the poor.
rows.anchor: ومنفعة القمار هو أن يفوز الرجل بمال صاحبه من غير كد ولا مشقة ويرتفق به الفقراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their sin outweighs their worldly benefit because it incurs God’s displeasure in the afterlife, leaving only a small, impermanent gain.
rows.anchor: لأن نفعهما في الدنيا وما يحصل من الإثم بهما يوجب سخط الله في الآخرة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan infers prohibition because harm exceeds benefit and because the verse calls it sin, which another verse forbids; its description as a major sin independently supports prohibition.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن: في الآية تحريم الخمر من وجهين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wine is called ithm in Arabic, as the cited poem shows; the verse’s description of it as a great sin also supports prohibition.
rows.anchor: شربت الإثم حتى ضل عقلي كذاك الإثم يصنع بالعقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the sin great is itself evidence of prohibition, since a major sin is prohibited without disagreement.
rows.anchor: الكبير محرم بلا خلاف

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak reads the comparison across time: after prohibition, their sin is greater than their benefit before prohibition.
rows.anchor: إثمهما بعد تحريمهما أكبر من نفعهما قبل تحريمهما

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿid ibn Jubayr says both refer to the pre-prohibition period: the sin caused by them exceeds their benefit.
rows.anchor: كلاهما قبل التحريم يعني أن الإثم الذي يحدث من أسبابهما أكبر من نفعهما

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says this verse does not establish prohibition; al-Maʾida 5:90 does.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة هذه الآية لا تدل على تحريمهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question means, “What thing should they spend?”
rows.anchor: أي أي شيء ينفقون

rows.speaker: عمرو بن الجموح
rows.claim: ʿAmr ibn al-Jamuh asked what should be spent in jihad; another report says the question concerned charity.
rows.anchor: السائل عمرو بن الجموح سأل عن النفقة في الجهاد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وقتادة
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and Qatada interpret al-ʿafw as what remains beyond family needs and sufficiency.
rows.anchor: ما فضل عن الأهل والعيال والفضل عن الغنى عن ابن عباس وقتادة

rows.speaker: الحسن وعطاء
rows.claim: Al-Hasan and ʿAtaʾ take al-ʿafw as the moderate amount, avoiding extravagance and stinginess; this is also transmitted from Abu Abd Allah.
rows.anchor: أن العفو الوسط من غير إسراف ولا إقتار عن الحسن وعطا وهو المروي عن أبي عبد الله

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر الباقر
rows.claim: Abu Jaʿfar al-Baqir says al-ʿafw is what remains after a year’s provisions; he says the zakat verse abrogated this, as al-Suddi also held.
rows.anchor: أن العفو ما فضل عن قوت السنة عن أبي جعفر الباقر ع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fourth, unattributed interpretation takes al-ʿafw to mean the finest and best property.
rows.anchor: أن العفو أطيب المال وأفضله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demonstrative’s kāf is singular because the address is to the Prophet, while including the community.
rows.anchor: إنما وحد الكاف لأن الخطاب للنبي ويدخل فيه الأمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another construal makes the address “thus, people of this group.”
rows.anchor: تقديره كذلك أيها القبيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The signs are proofs concerning spending, wine, and gambling.
rows.anchor: أي الحجج في أمر النفقة والخمر والميسر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation takes the signs to mean all the rulings of Islam.
rows.anchor: في سائر شرائع الإسلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here “this world and the hereafter” means their affairs.
rows.anchor: أي في أمر الدنيا وأمر الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pondering worldly and afterlife affairs shows that this life is trial, hardship, and passing, while the afterlife is recompense and permanence, prompting renunciation of one and desire for the other.
rows.anchor: فتعلمون أن الدنيا دار بلاء وعناء وفناء والآخرة دار جزاء وبقاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, “in this world and the hereafter” attaches to “He makes clear”: God explains signs in those matters so people ponder, showing He intends reflection whether or not they actually reflect.
rows.anchor: أي كما يبين لكم الآيات في الخمر والميسر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This continues Ibn Abbas’s account: after the warnings against orphan-property abuse, guardians separated food and drink from the orphans’, found this burdensome, and asked; the verse came down.
rows.anchor: انطلق كل من كان عنده يتيم فعزل طعامه من طعامه وشرابه من شرابه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question elides “caring for” orphans or managing their property, not their persons, since the answer does not concern who they are.
rows.anchor: ولا بد من إضمار في الكلام لأن السؤال لم يقع عن أشخاص اليتامى ولا ورد الجواب عنها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reform means improving orphans’ property without taking a fee from them, which is better and brings greater reward.
rows.anchor: إصلاح لأموالهم من غير أجرة عوض منهم خير وأعظم أجرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Guardians may mix assets to offset care costs and share food, drink, housing, and similar matters when pursuing the orphans’ welfare; al-Hasan and others and Imami reports transmit this permission.
rows.anchor: وهذا إذن لهم فيما كانوا يتحرجون منه من مخالطة الأيتام في الأموال من المأكل والمشرب والمسكن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God knows whether a guardian’s purpose in mixing with orphans is to corrupt or improve their property.
rows.anchor: والله يعلم من كان غرضه من مخالطة اليتامى إفساد مالهم أو إصلاح مالهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Had God willed, He would have constrained you in orphan matters and required the separation from their property you had been observing.
rows.anchor: أي لضيق عليكم في أمر اليتامى ومخالطتهم وألزمكم ما كنتم تجتنبونه

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj says God could have imposed what was difficult, thereby causing hardship, but did not.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: معناه لكلفكم ما يشق عليكم فتعنتون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse refutes the Mujabira: God did not will hardship and granted ease as a favor, so it is incoherent to claim He wills impossible burdens and commands what people cannot do.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا دلالة على بطلان قول المجبرة لأنه سبحانه إذا لم يشأ إعناتهم

rows.speaker: البلخي
rows.claim: Al-Balkhi says the verse refutes those who deny God’s power to do wrong: imposing an unjust burden is within divine power and could have been done if willed.
rows.anchor: قال البلخي وفيه أيضا دلالة على فساد من قال أنه تعالى لا يقدر على الظلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s might lets Him do as He wills without resistance; His actions and governance remain wise, with no impediment to what wisdom requires.
rows.anchor: يفعل بعزته ما يحب لا يدفعه عنه دافع

rows.speaker: أهل المدينة
rows.claim: The people of Medina retain the alif in ana when the following word begins with hamza carrying fatḥa or ḍamma; before hamza with kasra, readers unanimously drop it.
rows.anchor: قرأ أهل المدينة أنا أحيي بإثبات الألف في أنا والمد إذا كان بعدها همزة مضمومة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alif of ana is originally a pause marker, like the pause hāʾ in muslimūnah, and normally drops in connected speech.
rows.anchor: الأصل في أنا الهمزة والنون وإنما يلحقها الألف في الوقف كما أن الهاء تلحق للوقف

rows.speaker: الأعشى
rows.claim: Al-Aʿsha and another poet give examples of retaining the alif of ana in connected speech.
rows.anchor: نحو قول الأعشى: فكيف أنا وانتحال القوافي

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu Ali knows no distinction between hamza and other letters that would justify retaining an alif normally used only at pause.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي وما روي في إثبات الألف في أنا إذا كان بعد الألف همزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Buhita has four Arabic forms; the passive form buhita is the most eloquent and the reading used here.
rows.anchor: في بهت أربع لغات بهت على وزن ظرف وبهت على وزن حذر وبهت على وزن ذهب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Buhita means to be stopped and bewildered; the active verb can also mean confronting someone with a lie, since a defeated liar is confounded by proof.
rows.anchor: يقال بهت الرجل يبهت بهتا إذا انقطع وتحير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root links bewilderment under proof with false accusation; the same word appears in 4:20.
rows.anchor: فالبهت الحيرة عند استيلاء الحجة لأنها كالحيرة للمواجه بالكذب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Have you not seen” uses ila to express wonder at the disbeliever’s extraordinary false argument; sight reaches an unusual endpoint, almost functioning like a simile marker.
rows.anchor: إنما أدخلت إلى في الكلام للتعجب من حال الكافر المحاج بالباطل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After describing God as believers’ patron and the disbelievers’ patron as taghut, the passage consoles the Prophet with Abraham’s story.
rows.anchor: لما بين تعالى أنه ولي المؤمنين وإن الكفار لا ولي لهم سوى الطاغوت تسلية لنبيه

rows.speaker: مجاهد وغيره
rows.claim: The disputant is Nimrod son of Canaan, whom Mujahid and others call the first tyrant and claimant to divinity.
rows.anchor: وهو نمرود بن كنعان وهو أول من تجبر وادعى الربوبية عن مجاهد وغيره

rows.speaker: الصادق
rows.claim: Al-Sadiq places the dispute before Abraham’s idols were broken and before he was thrown into the fire made cool and safe for him.
rows.anchor: عند كسر الأصنام قبل إلقائه في النار وجعلها عليه بردا وسلاما عن الصادق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “About his Lord” means the Lord of Abraham, who called people to divine unity and worship.
rows.anchor: أي: في رب إبراهيم الذي يدعو إلى توحيده وعبادته

rows.speaker: الحسن والجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Hasan and al-Jubbaʾi take the pronoun as Nimrod: God gave him worldly rule and abundant wealth, and arrogance over this favor drove him to challenge Abraham.
rows.anchor: الهاء من أتاه تعود إلى المحاج لإبراهيم أي أعطاه الله الملك وهو نعيم الدنيا وسعة المال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worldly kingship may be granted to anyone, but God entrusts lawful rule, command, and binding obedience only to someone who calls to righteousness, never to a known corrupter.
rows.anchor: فأما الملك بتمليك الأمر والنهي وتدبير أمور الناس وإيجاب الطاعة على الخلق فلا يجوز

rows.speaker: أبو القاسم البلخي
rows.claim: Abu al-Qasim al-Balkhi takes the pronoun to refer to Abraham; Nimrod’s imprisoning and releasing people were coercive, while lawful authority belonged to Abraham from God.
rows.anchor: إلى إبراهيم عن أبي القاسم البلخي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The speech omits Nimrod’s question, “Who is your Lord?”, to which Abraham answers that his Lord gives life and death.
rows.anchor: في الكلام حذف وهو إذ قال له نمرود من ربك فقال ربي الذي يحيي ويميت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Life is named first as God’s first blessing; giving life and taking the soul without bodily injury or an action upon the body exceed human power and belong to God.
rows.anchor: بدأ بذكر الحياة لأنها أول نعمة ينعم الله بها على خلقه ثم يميتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nimrod claimed to give life by releasing a condemned prisoner and cause death by execution; this confuses words with creating life and death, which only God can do.
rows.anchor: أنا أحيي بالتخلية من الحبس من وجب عليه القتل وأميت بالقتل

words: فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَأْتِى بِٱلشَّمْسِ مِنَ ٱلْمَشْرِقِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation says Abraham did not abandon his first proof: a wise speaker may add a confirming argument once the initial proof is complete and no effective objection remains.
rows.anchor: إيراد حجة أخرى على سبيل التأكيد بعد تمام ما ابتدأ به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation says Abraham chose the clearer sign because listeners might mistake life and death for ordinary acts; prophets clarify truth rather than merely seek debate victory.
rows.anchor: أن إبراهيم إنما قال ذلك ليبين أن من شأن من يقدر

words: قَالَ إِبْرَٰهِۦمُ رَبِّىَ ٱلَّذِى يُحْىِۦ وَيُمِيتُ
rows.speaker: الصادق
rows.claim: Al-Sadiq says Abraham first challenged Nimrod to revive someone he had killed if truthful, then overcame him with the sun challenge.
rows.anchor: عن الصادق ع أن إبراهيم ع قال له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disbeliever was confounded when the decisive proof became manifest and he could not answer.
rows.anchor: أي تحير عند الانقطاع بما بان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One answer to why Nimrod did not ask Abraham’s Lord to bring the sun from the west is that he knew the miracle would affirm Abraham and expose him further.
rows.anchor: لما علم بما رأى من الآيات أنه لو اقترح ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second answer is that God forsook Nimrod and favored Abraham, leaving Nimrod unable to produce even a specious objection.
rows.anchor: أن الله خذله ولطف لإبراهيم حتى إنه لم يأت بشبهة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading is that God does not assist wrongdoers in reaching their corrupt aims.
rows.anchor: بالمعونة على بلوغ البغية من الفساد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading is that God does not guide wrongdoers in argument as He guides His prophets and friends.
rows.anchor: لا يهديهم إلى المحاجة كما يهدي أنبياءه وأولياءه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third reading is that God withholds His grace and support once He knows no gracious aid will benefit them.
rows.anchor: لا يهديهم بألطافه وتأييده إذا علم أنه لا لطف لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fourth reading takes the phrase to mean that God does not guide them to Paradise.
rows.anchor: لا يهديهم إلى الجنة وهذا لا يعارض قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This does not contradict that God guided Thamud: guidance has several senses, some general to all responsible people and some specific to believers, as explained at 2:26 and 41:17.
rows.anchor: معاني الهداية ووجوهها قبل عند قوله يضل به كثير ويهدى به كثيرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disputation shows that knowledge of the Creator is not innate or necessary; otherwise argument to establish the Creator would have no force.
rows.anchor: دلالة على أن المعارف غير ضرورية إذ لو كانت كذلك لما صحت المحاجة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse rejects blind imitation and affirms rational argument.
rows.anchor: دلالة على فساد التقليد وحسن الحجاج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is known through His acts that no one else can perform.
rows.anchor: وأنه تعالى إنما يعلم بأفعاله التي لا يقدر عليها غيره

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says God sent a mosquito against Nimrod; it entered his nostril and brain, tormented him for forty nights, and killed him.
rows.anchor: وفي تفسير ابن عباس: أن الله سبحانه سلط على نمرود بعوضة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah has five verses by consensus except in counting: Kufans count Alif-Lām-Mīm and omit “He sent down the Criterion,” while others do the reverse.
rows.anchor: خمس آيات بلا خلاف إلا أن الكوفي عد الم آية وترك وأنزل الفرقان

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر والأعشى والبرجمي
rows.claim: Abu Jaʿfar, al-Aʿsha, and al-Barjamī (from Abu Bakr, from ʿAsim) read the mīm still and separate Allah’s hamza; the majority connect the words and open the mīm.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو جعفر والأعشى والبرجمي عن أبي بكر عن عاصم الم الله بسكون الميم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Omitting the connecting alif in Allah shows the mīm is still; the pause-built letter names take fatḥa before a third consonant, like nūn in “fi Allāh.” A separated alif starts a new word after pausing.
rows.anchor: اتفاق الجميع على إسقاط الألف الموصولة في اسم الله تعالى دل على أن الميم ساكنة

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب وابن مسعود وإبراهيم النخعي والأعمش وزيد بن علي بن الحسين وجعفر بن محمد الصادق والنبي
rows.claim: An anomalous reading reported from these authorities, including the Prophet, has al-ḥayy al-qiyām instead of al-ḥayy al-qayyūm.
rows.anchor: وروي في الشواذ عن عمر بن الخطاب وابن مسعود وإبراهيم النخعي والأعمش

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan reads al-injīl with fatḥa on its initial hamza.
rows.anchor: عن الحسن: الإنجيل بفتح الهمزة

rows.speaker: ابن جني
rows.claim: Ibn Jinni derives al-qiyām from qāma on adjective pattern fīʿāl: its original yāʾ and still wāw met, the wāw changed into yāʾ and merged; al-qayyūm follows fīʿūl from the same source.
rows.anchor: قال ابن جني إنه صفة على فيعال من قام يقوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The open-initial-hamza form has no known Arabic parallel in afʿīl, but Tabarsi treats injīl as Arabic from najala, “extract”; the Gospel extracts knowledge of lawful matters, as al-Aʿsha’s cited line illustrates the root.
rows.anchor: لأنه ليس في كلامهم أفعيل بفتح الهمزة ولو كان أعجميا لكان فيه ضرب من الحجاج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One derivation takes tawrāt from kindling a fire: the initial wāw changes to tāʾ, and the name denotes bringing out what the book contains about licit and illicit matters.
rows.anchor: كما قيل توارة وهي فوعلة من وري الزند إذا قدح

rows.speaker: علي بن عيسى
rows.claim: Ali ibn Isa says injīl derives from najl meaning origin, so the Gospel is a foundation of knowledge.
rows.anchor: وقال علي بن عيسى: النجل الأصل فكأن الإنجيل أصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another etymology takes najl as offspring: the Gospel is a branch derived from the Torah.
rows.anchor: النجل الفرع ومنه قيل للولد نجل فكأن الإنجيل فرع على التوراة

rows.speaker: ابن فضال
rows.claim: Ibn Faddal derives injīl from najl, spaciousness; as with a wide eye or wound, the Gospel gives a wider allowance than the Torah.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن فضال هو من النجل وهو من السعة يقال عين نجلاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Musaḍḍiqan is accusative as a circumstantial accusative; min qabl, detached from its genitive construction, is built on ḍamm; hudan is a circumstantial accusative for Torah and Gospel or predicate of an omitted “they are.”
rows.anchor: مصدقا نصب على الحال وقوله من قبل أي من قبل إنزال الكتاب

rows.speaker: الكلبي ومحمد بن إسحاق والربيع بن أنس
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi, Ibn Ishaq, and al-Rabiʿ say the opening eighty-odd verses came down about Najran’s sixty-man delegation, whose fourteen notables included Aqib Abd al-Masih, Sayyid al-Ayham, and the bishop Abu Haritha.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي ومحمد بن إسحاق والربيع بن أنس " نزلت أوائل السورة إلى نيف وثمانين آية في وفد نجران

words: إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يَخْفَىٰ عَلَيْهِ شَىْءٌ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ وَلَا فِى ٱلسَّمَآءِ
rows.speaker: الكلبي ومحمد بن إسحاق والربيع بن أنس
rows.claim: The Christians rang a bell and prayed eastward in the Prophet’s mosque, which he permitted. His arguments that Jesus dies, depends on God, and knows only what is taught silenced them, and the opening verses were revealed.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي ومحمد بن إسحاق والربيع بن أنس " نزلت أوائل السورة إلى نيف وثمانين آية في وفد نجران

words: إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يَخْفَىٰ عَلَيْهِ شَىْءٌ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ وَلَا فِى ٱلسَّمَآءِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After warning against failing to know God despite proofs of His unity and the prophets’ truth, the verse warns that secret sins do not escape the Judge.
rows.anchor: لما ذكر سبحانه الوعيد على الإخلال بمعرفته مع نصب الأدلة على توحيده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Specifying earth and heaven stresses that hidden acts in either place are known, making the warning more vivid and weighty while also indicating God knows everything.
rows.anchor: لأن الغرض أن يعلمنا أنه يعلم ما يستسر به في الأرض أو في السماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saying nothing escapes God, rather than simply saying He knows everything on earth and in heaven, indicates knowledge of things in every knowable respect.
rows.anchor: لأن الوصف بأنه لا يخفى عليه شيء يدل على أنه يعلمه من كل وجه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God knows by His own essence; because everything knowable is known to Him, nothing can remain hidden in any respect.
rows.anchor: لأنه عالم لنفسه فيجب أن يعلم كل ما يصح أن يكون معلوما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kufans count Torah and Gospel together as one verse, not “Children of Israel”; others count “Children of Israel” but not the Gospel, preserving the continuation “and a messenger.”
rows.anchor: عد أهل الكوفة التوراة والإنجيل آية ولم يعدوا بني إسرائيل

rows.speaker: أهل المدينة وعاصم ويعقوب وسهل
rows.claim: Medina’s readers, ʿAsim, Yaʿqub, and Sahl read yuʿallimuhu with yāʾ; the remaining readers use nuʿallimuhu with nūn.
rows.anchor: قرأ أهل المدينة وعاصم ويعقوب وسهل ويعلمه بالياء والباقون بالنون

rows.speaker: نافع
rows.claim: Nafiʿ reads innī akhluqu with kasra on the hamza; other readers use fatḥa.
rows.anchor: قرأ نافع إني أخلق بكسر الألف والباقون أني بالفتح

rows.speaker: أهل المدينة ويعقوب وأبو جعفر
rows.claim: Medina and Yaʿqub read ṭāʾiran; Abu Jaʿfar reads ka-hayʾat al-ṭāʾir in both places; other readers have ṭayran without alif.
rows.anchor: قرأ أهل المدينة ويعقوب طائرا ومثله في المائدة وأبو جعفر كهيئة الطائر فيهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The yāʾ reading links “he teaches him” to God’s good news; the nūn reading follows the first-person plural pattern “We decreed death.”
rows.anchor: من قرأ ويعلمه عطفه على قوله إن الله يبشرك ومن قرأ ونعلمه جعله على نحو نحن قدرنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With fatḥa, annī is appositional to āya; with kasra it may begin a new clause or explain the sign, the latter being better because it has the same sense as apposition.
rows.anchor: ومن كسر أحتمل وجهين أحدهما: الاستئناف وقطع الكلام مما قبله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The singular ṭāʾiran can describe each thing shaped and breathed into as a bird, as “flog them eighty lashes” means eighty lashes for each person.
rows.anchor: ومن قرأ طائرا أراد فيكون ما أنفخ فيه أو ما أخلقه طائرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥikma and ḥukm have the same meaning.
rows.anchor: الحكمة والحكم بمعنى ونظيره الذلة والذل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source notes ordinary ṭīn, using clay to seal a letter and coating a house with clay as examples of the related verb ṭayyana.
rows.anchor: والطين معروف وطنت الكتاب جعلت عليه طينا لأختمه به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hayʾa means the visible state or form of something.
rows.anchor: والهيئة الحال الظاهرة هاء فلان يهاء هيئة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nafkh means blowing, and naffākha can refer to a bubble of water.
rows.anchor: والنفخ معروف نفخ ينفخ نفخا والنفاخة للماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-akmah means the blind; Suwayd ibn Abi Kahil’s poem depicts eyes becoming white.
rows.anchor: قال سويد بن أبي كاهل:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iddikhār is an iftiʿāl verbal noun from d-kh-r; grammarians also permit tadhkharūn with dhāl.
rows.anchor: والادخار الافتعال من الدخر وجوز النحويون تذخرون بالذال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yaʿallimuhu may coordinate with wajīhan or with a complete clause; attaching it to nūḥīhi is rejected because that leaves Mary’s good-news context.
rows.anchor: موضع يعلمه يحتمل أن يكون نصبا بالعطف على وجيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rasūlan is accusative after an omitted “and We make him,” or as a circumstantial phrase for his future mission; al-Zajjaj paraphrases it as speaking to them as a messenger.
rows.anchor: ورسولا نصب على تقدير ونجعله رسولا فحذف لدلالة البشارة عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Annī akhluqu can be genitive as apposition to āya or nominative; al-Zajjaj says the kasra reading means “I say: I have come to you.”
rows.anchor: وموضع أني أخلق لكم يحتمل أن يكون خفضا ورفعا فالخفض على البدل من آية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mā can be a relative pronoun (“what you eat and store”) or a verbal noun (“your eating and storing”); the relative reading is better.
rows.anchor: وبما تأكلون جائز أن يكون ما هنا بمعنى الذي أي بما تأكلونه وتدخرونه
